memory_candidates.content: This codebase's commands/skills are markdown-defined and executed literally by the agent following their embedded jq/bash snippets -- there is no compiled script for many state.json writers. A grep restricted to *.sh when checking 'does anything write field X on state.json' will miss real, live writers embedded in commands/*.md or skills/*/SKILL.md (confirmed for active_goal in commands/review.md and previous_status in skills/skill-spawn/SKILL.md). Always grep *.md alongside *.sh when establishing 'no writer found' for a state.json field.

A context/patterns/*.md file being actively cross-referenced by other live docs does not mean every jq/bash snippet inside it is still executed by a current skill -- individual snippets within an otherwise-live file can be vestigial/superseded (e.g. jq-escaping-workarounds.md's 'researched: $ts' Research Postflight template vs. skill-status-sync/SKILL.md's actual postflight_update operation, which omits that field). Verify at the operation level (the skill's actual Execution steps), not just at the file-reference level, before concluding a documented write pattern is live.

When a consumer repo's state.json carries top-level bookkeeping fields (metadata{generated_at,total_tasks,last_sync}, task_counts, stray top-level artifacts/last_updated) that no current agent-system script reads or writes, check git history with `git log -S'<field>' -- specs/state.json` before ruling: this repeatedly surfaced a pre-agent-system generator/tooling era whose output is now manually, ad-hoc reconciled by the consumer repo's own maintainer (who had already independently started retiring the same field family by hand, e.g. task_counts). That history is strong, fast evidence for a (c) RETIRE ruling versus guessing from static grep alone.
